summary:
AURORA is a lunar geospatial platform designed to evaluate and compare candidate landing sites against mission-specific requirements.
It brings together multiple dimensions of lunar science and mission analysis, transforming fragmented information into a cohesive intelligence framework that enables more informed and comprehensive mission decisions.
 Users can define mission requirements, examine candidate locations and evaluate their suitability through hard constraints and weighted preferences with transparent explanations of trade-offs and missing evidence.
details:
AURORA helps users determine which candidate lunar sites merit further consideration for a given mission. Developed for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, it brings terrain suitability, solar-power potential and direct-to-Earth communication visibility into a unified assessment. By evaluating these factors against mission requirements and available evidence, AURORA enables users to compare site trade-offs and identify gaps requiring further investigation before making informed decisions.

What users can do:

- Explore the lunar south pole. Rotate, zoom, and reset a 3D Moon with NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera imagery and Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter relief. Find sites through search or use the south-polar 2D projection to move between Shackleton, Malapert, Haworth, and Amundsen candidates. Review site coordinates and switch to a terrain cutout to inspect local relief.

- Set mission requirements. Start from a mission category or edit six requirements directly: maximum footprint slope, maximum roughness, minimum Sun visibility, maximum continuous darkness, minimum valid terrain coverage, and minimum valid temporal illumination coverage. Users can preview a category’s recommendations and apply them deliberately. The guided workflow leads from mission setup to selection and evidence review.

- Evaluate, inspect, and compare sites. Python evaluates the selected sites against a shared set of applied requirements. The map, Site Inspector, and comparison views display the outcome and its evidence. Users can see the measured value, the allowed limit, which mandatory checks passed or failed, and how each criterion contributed to an eligible site’s score.

- Review terrain, lighting, and mobility. The site panels expose terrain statistics, Sun visibility, continuous darkness, and a permanently shadowed region indicator where supported by the preview. Rover previews show route geometry, distance, travel time, and drive energy on a synthetic terrain grid. Saved approach and surface simulation records illustrate corridor geometry, operating windows, energy and battery budgets, timeline events, and requirement checks.

- Explore trade-offs beyond one score. The mission trade study compares landing suitability, mobility, energy survival, and science return. It uses a Pareto comparison to identify options that excel on different priorities. For example, a site can improve science access while demanding a harder traverse.

The trade-study interface also provides JSON and Markdown export controls.

- Control the visual timeline. Step the UTC preview by ±6 or ±24 hours, or play and pause it at 1×, 2×, 4×, and 8× demo speed. The globe turns in proportion to elapsed simulated time using the Moon’s mean sidereal rotation rate. The clock makes the change in orientation visible while site-specific mission-date calculations remain a separate scientific workflow. NASA Moon Fact Sheet

How the assessment works

The Next.js Explorer sends the candidate identity and applied mission requirements to a Python FastAPI service. The backend first checks mandatory conditions and evidence coverage. An eligible site receives a weighted score out of 100. A site that fails a mandatory condition, or has insufficient mandatory evidence, receives a withheld score and an explanation.

The default weights are 25% for 95th-percentile slope, 20% for roughness, 25% for direct illumination, 15% for continuous darkness, and 15% for evidence confidence. The maximum slope is also subject to a separate mandatory check. That distinction matters: a favorable overall slope distribution cannot compensate for a maximum slope that exceeds the mission limit.

Controlled Shackleton Ridge Peak Alpha test Result

Maximum footprint slope set to 10° 62.93 / 100

Same site and evidence, limit relaxed to 20° 71.80 / 100

Same site and evidence, limit tightened to 3° Score withheld

Terrain coverage across all three runs 100 valid cells out of 100

The test demonstrates Aurora’s central design choice: the mission requirement can change the verdict while the evidence stays the same. This gives reviewers a reproducible way to test the decision rather than relying on a score in isolation.

Scientific engineering and validation

- Terrain processing. Aurora’s backend validates staged raster files against their expected identity, checksum, coordinate frame, resolution, and pixel registration. It reads bounded windows from verified elevation rasters and accounts for missing or unsupported samples in coverage. The research pipeline also examines how fine local terrain and broader regional elevation products can support different parts of a horizon calculation.

- Real terrain control. On a separate 100 m-radius footprint from the 3.5 m/pixel Shackleton–de Gerlache Connecting Ridge elevation model, the documented control run found 2,561 valid cells out of 2,565 and a 95th-percentile slope of 21.94°. This footprint is distinct from the Shackleton Alpha demonstration site. It verifies the extraction and coverage calculation for that particular footprint.

- Sun and Earth geometry. The backend includes SPICE-based lunar geometry and terrain-horizon calculations. In documented comparisons with NASA JPL Horizons, the maximum angular separation across 60 selected Sun and Earth geometry samples was approximately 0.12 arcseconds. This is agreement for the tested geometry cases. Terrain-obstructed visibility and landing suitability require their own validation.

- Time, coordinates, and missing evidence. Scientific calculations distinguish user-facing UTC from ephemeris time and use explicit lunar reference frames. Terrain, temporal illumination, and spatial illumination coverage are tracked separately. A spatially unresolved or missing observation stays unknown.

What the current release demonstrates

The interactive globe uses NASA-derived imagery and relief. The public assessment and terrain, lighting, and traverse demonstrations use labeled synthetic evidence. The Approach and Simulation panels show saved reference scenarios. The research backend contains the terrain and geometry components for real-site analysis. The next milestone is to connect verified terrain and ephemeris inputs for the same site, footprint, and mission window, then expose independently checked Sun and direct-to-Earth visibility windows.

Intended impact and technology

Aurora makes lunar planning trade-offs accessible in a browser. A student can see why stricter limits change a verdict. An educator can show why good data coverage and a good operational outcome are separate questions. An early-stage mission team can use the same workflow to decide what to investigate next.

The Explorer uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Three.js. The scientific backend uses Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, NumPy, Rasterio/GDAL, and SpiceyPy. Shared schemas and Vitest, pytest, Playwright, and GitHub Actions support repeatable verification. The project runs on standard computers with a browser and a Python service.

Business Model-

AURORA Labs empowers science communicators and exploration facilitators seeking more engaging and interactive ways to bring lunar science to their audiences. It also caters to Researchers and Exploration Aficionados seeking to delve deeper into lunar science and exploration, offering advanced geospatial capabilities and detailed mission analysis to investigate the Moon beyond surface-level understanding.

AURORA Enterprise empowers organisations operating at the frontier of lunar exploration with mission-specific geospatial intelligence to evaluate candidate sites against complex operational requirements enabling more informed decisions throughout mission development and execution.

FUTURE EXPANSION & POSITIONING-

AURORA aims to evolve beyond site assessment into a specialised lunar decision-intelligence platform, extending its capabilities across scientific research, mission simulation and mission-level analysis.

01 - Agentic Research Infrastructure

Developing agentic capabilities to conduct specialised scientific research across lunar domains, enabling organisations to undertake multidisciplinary research with leaner teams and reduced specialist manpower.

02 - Lunar Mission Simulation Infrastructure

Creating a virtual lunar environment to recreate mission conditions, test operational scenarios and support research and training for future lunar specialists.

03 - Lunar Knowledge Model

Building an evolving knowledge system that learns from historical lunar missions, extracting insights to inform future mission objectives, architectures and operational requirements.
